title: The GNSS Spoofing Crisis Is a Cockpit Software Problem, Not Just a Navigation Hardware Story
summary: GNSS spoofing events have spread from Eastern Europe to the Gulf, the Baltic, and Southeast Asia at a pace the flight ops software stack has not matched — and the industry keeps framing it as a hardware and airspace management issue when the real gap is in pilot-facing tools.
body_markdown:
GNSS spoofing has been climbing the aviation safety agenda for three years, but the numbers coming out of recent reporting make the scale of the problem hard to ignore any longer. IATA's 2025 Annual Safety Report documented a 67% rise in GNSS jamming incidents and a 193% increase in spoofing events between 2023 and 2025, spreading well beyond the original concentration around Eastern Europe and the Black Sea into the Baltic, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East. OPSGROUP's tracking puts the Gulf corridor in particularly sharp relief: by March 2026, more than 700 flights in Gulf air routes had reportedly experienced suspected spoofing events.

Those are not edge-case statistics. They describe a phenomenon affecting mainstream commercial air corridors at a rate that has become, by any reasonable measure, a routine operational hazard. And yet if you look at where the aviation software industry is directing its energy in response, you mostly find hardware conversations — inertial navigation system upgrades, alternative positioning systems, antenna-level mitigations — rather than a serious reckoning with what the cockpit information layer needs to do differently.

That framing is wrong, and I think it's costing the industry time it doesn't have.

## The Cockpit Software Stack Has a GNSS Dependency It Rarely Acknowledges

Flight planning tools, EFB platforms, and onboard navigation displays have all been designed around the assumption that GNSS position data is authoritative — or at worst, that discrepancies will be caught by cross-checking against inertial reference systems. What the spoofing environment has revealed is that those cross-checks aren't always fast enough, visible enough to the crew, or surfaced in a way that prompts the right response at the right moment.

The harder-to-acknowledge truth is that most EFB platforms and digital cockpit tools have no coherent answer to the question: what does a pilot see, and what does the software recommend, when GNSS integrity can't be trusted? The preflight briefing workflow doesn't systematically flag airspace corridors with elevated spoofing risk. In-flight moving map applications render position data without communicating the confidence level of that position. Route planning tools don't automatically surface alternate navigation strategies when a flight transits a known high-risk corridor.

Some of this is genuinely hard to solve — spoofing events aren't always predictable in time and place, and the sensor fusion problem is legitimately complex. But the software dimension is solvable faster than the hardware dimension, and the industry isn't treating it with that urgency.

## This Is Exactly the Kind of Problem Pilot-Facing Software Should Be Designed to Surface

Having spent years working across flight planning platforms and navigation data products, the thing that strikes me most about the GNSS spoofing problem is how well it maps to what EFB and digital cockpit tools are supposed to be for. The whole premise of a pilot-facing operational intelligence layer is that it aggregates external information — NOTAMs, weather, airspace restrictions, route optimization data — and presents it to the crew in a way that supports better decisions. GNSS threat corridors are exactly that kind of information.

There are vendors starting to move in this direction. OPSGROUP has built corridor risk awareness tools that operators can subscribe to. Some flight planning platforms are beginning to incorporate GNSS-threat corridor data into their briefing products. But this is not yet standard. It's not baked into the EFB workflows where pilots actually spend their preflight time, and it's not integrated into the en-route advisory layer in any consistent way across the major platforms.

The argument I keep hearing against faster progress here is that the data is uncertain — threat corridor boundaries shift, spoofing events are hard to predict with precision. That's true. But we don't withhold turbulence forecasts because they're imprecise. We present probabilistic information with appropriate confidence framing and let crews factor it into their situational awareness. There's no principled reason GNSS threat data should be treated differently.

The spoofing numbers are no longer surprising — they're routine. The software industry's response to that routineness is what needs to catch up.

questions: When you were working on flight planning products, was GNSS integrity ever treated as a first-class input to the route briefing workflow — or was it always assumed to be an avionics-layer problem that the software didn't need to surface? (First-class input / Avionics-layer assumption / Varied by vendor)

In your view, is the main reason EFB platforms haven't integrated GNSS threat corridor data more aggressively: (a) the data quality isn't reliable enough yet, (b) it's been categorized as a hardware/avionics problem rather than a software problem, (c) there's no regulatory requirement pushing vendors to act, or (d) something else?

OPSGROUP has been doing the most visible work on operational GNSS threat awareness for crews — does that feel like the right place for this to originate, or should a major EFB or flight planning platform have stepped up first?

If you were defining the minimum viable GNSS-aware feature set for a modern EFB platform today, what would it need to include — preflight corridor flagging, in-flight confidence indication, something else?

Does the 193% spoofing increase number surprise you given what you've seen in the field, or does it track with the threat environment you were already aware of? (Surprising / Not surprising / Worse than I expected)

Today's post takes the position that the industry has been framing this as a navigation hardware and airspace management problem when the real gap is in pilot-facing software: EFB platforms and digital cockpit tools haven't integrated GNSS threat corridor awareness into standard preflight briefing or en-route advisory workflows in any consistent way. This is directly relevant right now because the spoofing rate has crossed from edge-case into routine operational hazard territory, and the software vendors who could act fastest — EFB and flight planning platform developers — are not visibly prioritizing it the way the numbers would justify.
